member of the Progressive party or any member of the Labour party; they all agreed that this was the proper method of procedure.
2.	Your committee recognizes that, while it is highly desirable that such legislation should be uniform in all the provinces, and while social insurance has a federal aspect, nevertheless, according to the Department of Justice, under our constitution legislative jurisdiction in relation to the establishment of a compulsory system of unemployment insurance is vested exclusively in the provincial legislatures.
And the present Prime Minister may I add was a party to the acceptance of the report.
3.	Your committee finds that the provinces, on being consulted by the Department of Labour with regard to their attitude towards the establishment of a general scheme, do not appear to be prepared to take immediate action.
4.	L'nder these circumstances, your committee submits the following recommendations:-*
(a)	That with regard to sickness insurance, the Department of Pensions and National Health be requested to initiate a comprehensive survey of the field of public health, with special reference to a national health program. In this, it is believed that it would be possible to secure the cooperation of the provincial and municipal health departments, as well the organized medical profession.
(b)	That in the forthcoming census, provision should be made for the securing of the fullest possible data regarding the extent of unemployment and sickness, and that this should be compiled and published at as early a date as possible.
(c)	That the federal government be requested to bring the subject matter of this reference before the next federal-provincial conference; and your committee suggests, when the agenda for such a conference is being arranged that the provincial governments be invited to send representatives of the employer and employee to discuss the subject matter of this report.
All of which was respectfully submitted and the report carried unanimously. That brings the matter of unemployment insurance up to 1929. In order to make it clear that the government of the day did not leave the matter there, but proceeded further, I have in my hand some correspondence in reply to communications sent out >by the Department of Labour to the different provinces on this matter in accordance with the recommendation of the committee. I shall read only one communication, and if the house will permit I shall place on Hansard the memorandum attached to it. The letter that I wish to read is one from the office of the premier of Saskatchewan, dated May 21,1930, a time when that office was filled by a Conservative premier. I take this communication because it comes as near to the time at which the 
Liberal administration left office as any of the correspondence, showing that up to the last minute we were seeking to get the cooperation of the provinces with respect to an unemployment insurance measure. I give it to the house also for another reason; an effort has been made in a very subtle way to make it appear that objection to this parliament proceeding in this matter has been coming from certain provincial administrations that happen to be Liberal. May I point out, as I did the other day, that no one was more emphatic in respect to no interference with provincial rights than the Hon. Howard Ferguson, who is to-day the high commissioner in London for the present administration. When the present government itself was dealing with the question of the statute of Westminster, even while the matter was in Tory hands, Hon. Howard Ferguson as Conservative premier of Ontario insisted that certain safeguards should be put into that measure in order that provincial rights in Ontario might not be invaded.
Here is the communication of Mr. J. T. M. Anderson, the Conservative premier of Saskatchewan of that day:
Premier's Office Saskatchewan
Regina, May 21, 1930. The Honourable Mr. Peter Heenan,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir,-With further reference to your letter of March 10th with respect to insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity, I wish to say that I have received an opinion from our Attorney General's Department which indicates that this matter falls within the competency of the provincial legislature. It would appear, then, that while any general scheme of compulsory insurance along the lines mentioned appears to be entirely a matter for provincial legislation there would seem to be no valid reason why the dominion might not cooperate by way of legislation for a grant of a sum of money in furtherance thereof.
1 would be very glad to know the attitude of your government in this connection.
For your information I am sending you a copy of the memorandum sent me by our Attorney General.
Yours faithfully.
(Sgd.) J. T. M. Anderson.
Then if the house will permit I shall place the accompanying memorandum on Hansard. It is a memorandum of the Hon. M. A. MacPherson:
Memorandum for the Honourable M. A. MacPherson, K.C.
Re: Legislative jurisdiction regarding a compulsory scheme of insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity.
I have the honour to refer to the above constitutional question as outlined in the recent correspondence between the Honourable J. T. M. Anderson. Premier of Saskatchewan, and the Honourable Peter Heenan, Minister of Labour

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Mackenzie King
in the dominon cabinet, from which it appears that you have been requested to prepare a legal opinion as to whether legislation to this end falls within the competency of a provincial legislature.
In dealing with the subject I think it right to premise, in the absence of any bill or proposed statute containing a definite scheme, that the opinion now given is with respect to legislation following the lines as set out on page 1 (IV) of the final report of the select standing committee of the House of Commons of Canada on industrial and international relations published in 1928, namely, that embodying the principle of insurance based on compulsory contributions derived from the state, the employer and the employee.
In accordance with the dicta of the judicial committee of the privy council as expounded on various occasions, the first question to be determined is whether such provincial legislation would fall within any of the classes of subjects enumerated in section 92 of the B.N.A. Act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces; for, if not, it can be of no validity and no other question would arise. It is only when an act of the provincial legislature prima facie falls within one of these classes of subjects that the further questions arise, namely, whether, notwithstanding this is so, the subject of the act does not also fall within one of the enumerated classes of section 91 and whether the power of the provincial legislature is not thereby overborne. See Citizens v. Parsons, 7 A.C. 109.
Having proceeded in accordance with the above dicta to examine sections 91 and 92 of The Confederation Act, I find that the subject of compulsory insurance along the lines indicated would, in my opinion, fall directly within clause 13 of section 92, namely, "property and civil rights in the province," one of the classes of subjects with respect to which exclusive jurisdiction has been relegated to provincial legislatures. Turning next to section 91, I have been unable to find that it comes under anv of the enumerated classes of that section. Further, it is now well settled that the general authority to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, which the initial part of section 91 of The British North America Act confers, does not, unless the subject matter of legislation falls within some of the enumerated heads which follow enable the dominion parliament to trench on the subject matters entrusted to the provincial legislatures by the enumeration in section 92 of the act. Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for Alberta and Attornev-General for British Columbia, 26 D.L.R. 288.
In Citizens v. Parsons (supra) an Ontario act was under review, namely, 39 Viet. Ch. 24. It dealt with policies of insurance entered into or in force in Ontario for insuring property situate therein against fire and prescribing certain conditions which were to form part of such contract. The judicial committee declared it to be valid legislation applicable to the contracts of all such insurers in Ontario, including corporations and companies, whatever might be their origin whether incorporated by British authority or by foreign or colonial authority. At page 111 their lordships, referring to 14 Geo. Ill, c. 83, a statute making provision for the government of Quebec, say:
"In this statute the words 'property' and 'civil rights' are plainly used in their largest sense, and there is no reason for holding that in the statute under discussion they are used in a different and narrower one.
The next question for consideration is whether, assuming the Ontario act to relate to the subject of property and civil rights, its enactment and provisions come within any of the classes of subjects enumerated in Section 91, the only one which the appellants suggest as expressly including the subject of the Ontario act is No. 2 'the regulation of trade and commerce.' "
It was held, however, that the words "regulation of trade and commerce" include political arrangements in regard to trade requiring the sanction of parliament, regulation of trade in matters of inter-provincial concern, and it may be, general regulation of trade affecting the whole dominion; but do not include the regulation of the contracts of a particular business or trade such as the business of fire insurance in a single province, and, therefore, do not conflict with the power of property and civil rights conferred by section 92, No. 13.
It appears to me to be clear that legislation setting up a scheme of compulsory insurance against employment, sickness and invalidity, requiring contributions from the state, the employer and employee would of necessity deal directly and primarily with the property and civil rights of individuals in the province affected, and while the constitutionality of legislation covering this particular species of insurance has not been directly determined by the eourts, I see no reason to doubt that the principles adopted in Citizens v. Parsons would apply. I am accordingly of the opinion that the exclusive jurisdiction to enact compulsory insurance legislation of this nature rests with the provinces.	_
Again, in Attorney-General for Canada against Attorney-General for Alberta and Attorney-General for British Columbia (insurance case) (supra) their lordships of the privy council held in effect that it was within the exclusive competence of provincial legislatures to legislate regarding the business of insurance. At page 292, 26 D.L.R. (supra) their lordships, in answer to the argument that the dominion had jurisdiction under section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, "trade and commerce" say:
" No doubt the business of insurance is a very important one which has attained to great dimensions in Canada, but this is equally true of other highly important and extensive forms of business in Canada which are to-day freely transacted under provincial authority. Where the B.N.A. Act has taken such forms of business out of provincial jurisdiction, as in the case of banking, it has done so by express words which would have been unnecessary had the argument for the dominion government addressed to this board from the bar been well-founded."	_
Turning now to a consideration of the question of insurance as viewed from the aspect of its relation to unemployment and sickness, the first of which would appear to come within the scope of legislation regarding labour in industrial undertakings, and the latter of which would appear to fall within the category of public

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Mackenzie King
health, the legislative jurisdiction in regard to these matters also in my opinion belongs primarily to the province.
In a reference by the Governor General of Canada to the Supreme court in the matter of legislative jurisdiction over hours of labour (1925), S.C.E. 505, the court held, inter alia:
" That the matter of labour in industrial undertakings in Canada is primarily within the competence of provincial legislatures, but parliament can legislate as to labour in territories not yet organized into, or forming part of, a province and as to labour of servants of the dominion if these are within the scope of the draft convention."
It appears to be only necessary to explain that the draft convention referred to was that adopted by the International Conference of the League of Nations in 1919 limiting the hours of labour in industrial undertakings.
Reference may also be made in this connection to In re the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act, 1919 (1922) 1 W.W.R. page 20, in which ease the privy council held the enactment of 'the above two acts to be ultra vires the dominion parliament. They were designed to prohibit undue combination and hoarding and the committee held their provisions to be an interference with the power to restrict the "civil rights" of the inhabitants of a province, a power exclusively relegated to provincial legislatures by the B.N.A. Act. See page 24 of the report (supra).
I would further refer to the judgment of the privy council in two cases which have particular application to the subject in hand, namely, "In re Reciprocal Insurance Legislation (1924) A.C. 328; (1914) 2 W.W.R. 397, and Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider et al (1925) 1 W.W.R. 785. In the case last referred to their lordships held the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act 1927 (Ch. 20, Dom.), ultra vires of the dominion parliament declaring it to be a law relating to matters as to which section 92 of the B.N.A. Act gives exclusive jurisdiction to the provinces. It was also held, approving the board's ruling in In re Reciprocal Insurance Legislation (supra), that the said act could not be justified as an exercise of the dominion's powers under section 91 of the B.N.A. Act with respect to criminal law, or with respect to the peace, order and good government of Canada. It was further held that the mere fact that legislation is for the general advantage of Canada or is such that it will meet a mere want felt throughout the dominion does not render it intra vires of the dominion parliament if it cannot be brought under the heads specifically enumerated in section 91 of the B.N.A. Act unless it is passed because of some extraordinary peril to the national life as a whole, such as a war or, perhaps, an epidemic of pestilence and that the evidence in the case at bar did not show such.
Again, the subject matter of public health appears to me clearly to fall within provincial legislative competence under the heading "property and civil rights" and might also be so claimed under item 16 of section 92 of the B.N.A. Act as being a matter of a local or private nature. There is also item 7 whereby exclusive legislative jurisdiction is conferred on the provinces respecting the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, etc., other than "marine hospitals" jurisdiction with respect to which has been specifically conferred upon the dominion by item II of section 91,

namely, "quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals." I am unable to find any other express heading of section 91 which would support the contention that public health generally is a matter of exclusive dominion jurisdiction. With regard to the opening words of section 91 conferring upon the dominion jurisdiction to enact laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, as has been shown, these words do not, unless the subject matters also fall within one of the enumerated heads of section 91, enable the parliament of Canada to trench on matters exclusively relegated to the provinces under section 92.
For the above reasons and on the above authorities, in my opinion the power to enact compulsory legislation with respect to insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity rests with the provinces.
I might add, however, that while any general scheme of compulsory insurance along the lines indicated appears to be entirely a matter for provincial legislation there would seem to be no valid reason why the dominion might not cooperate by way of legislation for the grant of a sum of money in furtherance thereof.
Alex. Blackwood,
Law Officer.
The point I wish to make clear is that this correspondence indicates an objection raised by a Conservative premier of one province saying that the dominion was invading its jurisdiction in seeking, as regards an unemployment insurance scheme, to do other than make a contribution to the province. Should we not have raised one of the greatest issues ever raised in this country if we had attempted to do what the Prime Minister to-day is attempting to do, if we had sought to defy those provincial governments with respect to their rights? We felt that whatever was to be done, to be effective, should be done in the right way and in accordance with the jurisdiction of parliament 'as it is known to exist.
I think I have made fairly clear why the government or any government between 1921 and 1930 could not have gone further than we did in the matter of social legislation, and in particular, with respect to any scheme of unemployment insurance. We had moved steadily ahead, we had carried all parties in this house with us every step of the way. There was as regards procedure no difference of opinion between Liberal, Conservative, Progressive or Labour; all were united in the steps we were taking. By advancing in that way we were taking a course that in the long run promised both certainty and security.
Now we come to the period when the present Prime Minister came into office. The first question I would again ask is: Why have we had to wait until 1935 to have some further step taken, some measure of social insurance

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Mackenzie King
introduced? Well, the Prime Minister gave one reason, I do not think it is a very good one, in his second radio address on January 4:
Row that we have achieved some measure of control over economic conditions and can operate without fear of imminent disaster we are going to do away as quickly as possible with emergency relief measures and put in a permanent system of sound and scientific insurance against unemployment.
He has not done away with any emergency relief measures as yet. I agree with the Prime Minister that the question of unemployment insurance is an entirely different matter from the question of relief. Unemployment insurance as introduced to-day relates to the future, to a time considerably in the future; unemployment relief relates to the present, and it is the present about which the people are concerned. What the people are demanding from this government is that present conditions shall be remedied, knowing full well that unless they are remedied no legislation in the world with respect to unemployment insurance is likely ever to become of any service to anyone. But when the Prime Minister undertook to say that he was not able to deal with this matter until he got control of the economic situation, I think he was going a little too far. Has he got control of the situation yet? Has he got control of the econmic conditions of the country? Is everything prosperous and going ahead? I do not believe the public share any such view. There was nothing in the situation from 1930 to prevent his going ahead with a national unemployment insurance scheme except the reasons he himself gave and which I shall quote in a few moments.
May I point out what attitude we of the official opposition took? Did we say, We think that because this is a period of depression we should not touch any social legislation until we get out of this period? Or did we say: This is the time of all times to settle these questions as to procedure and jurisdiction so that when the moment does come that we have reached an understanding with the provinces which will permit of the introduction of a system of national unemployment insurance no time will be lost in getting it placed upon the statute books? Did we not state over and over again that we believed that what in part was needed for dealing with unemployment as it might arise in the future was a national unemployment insurance scheme? We took the ground always that along with any measure of the kind there would have to be policies which would serve to revive industry and trade, and that in the meantime as long as we had the problem of relief on our hands it
would have to have immediate attention, the permanent as contrasted with the temporary measures going along parallel with them if you like. The point we stressed over and over again was that, while we were in a period of depression, we could at least settle the question of jurisdiction, we could at least bring the provinces into conference and work out something, and that that was the way in which the government should proceed. In 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934, every one of these years, we urged that a national unemployment insurance scheme should be introduced. We had been working on such a scheme, as I have shown, before leaving office in 1930. I shall not quote to any extent from what was said, only enough to verify the statement I have just made. In the House of Commons on April 29, 1931, at page 1113 of Hansard I am reported as follows:
As unemployment is incidental to industry as it is carried on to-day, I believe some system of insurance against unemployment is absolutely necessary and should be provided.
That was in 1931. Then on the next page:
having regard to the problem of unemployment before us at the moment, a problem that we know is going to recur from time to time, the government should immediately consider how a system of unemployment insurance can be made applicable to help meet such a situation.
Not consider in 1935, but "immediately" consider. Then further:
We have at the present time a federal system of annuities. I see no reason why the administration should not consider whether some advantage might not be taken of the annuity system already in existence as a federal system so to extend it as to make the moneys paid in as premiums available at times of unemployment, as unemployment insurance to those who make contributions towards it. It might be so extended as to make the system available to its contributors as insurance against sickness or invalidity. There is an opportunity for an immediate step to be taken by the federal government to provide a measure of unemployment insurance. Xo question of constitutionality can be raised with respect to it. I submit the government might well consider whether the system of providing annuities which now for many years has been administered by the federal government, might not be so extended in its bearing upon social problems, as to make it available to meet other risks that arise from industry.
There, I submit, was a constructive idea and suggestion. The Prime Minister says he has met with nothing but opposition from this side of the house. Has he listened to what we have been saying over and over again, from year to year urging the very sort of thing he now says he is trying to do in the bill he

In 1931 we saw very clearly that the considerations I have mentioned, with regard to financial jurisdiction, conference with the provinces and the like, would have to be considered, together with the necessity for the amendment of the British North America Act. Those factors we brought to the attention of the government. The amendment of the British North America Act was one point that was clear from the start. We have all seen, understanding the jurisdiction to be as we all along have believed it to be, that, if a national scheme of unemployment insurance was to be drawn up, it could be done only in one of two ways. One way was by agreement with the provinces whereby they would act within their jurisdiction and the government of Canada would contribute grants in aid, as has been done in the case of old age pensions; the other way was by amending the British North America Act in a manner that would enable this federal parliament alone to deal with the question. We always said that a conference with the provinces, if properly carried on, would enable us to reach agreement on an amendment of the British North America Act, but five years have been lost in the holding of any conference of the kind. I say here that we will yet discover that such a conference must take place; we will yet discover, before any legislation of this character comes within the jurisdiction of the federal government, that it will have to be by the path of some conference between the dominion and the provinces, and through agreement reached as a result thereof. I pointed out the desirability of a national scheme in dealing with old age pensions as part of a social insurance scheme:
... we believe old age pensions should be a part of the social insurance scheme of this country. But we think it should be a national scheme; it should be administered nationally, 100 per cent of the money raised and the entire scheme administered by the federal government.
We as Liberals were not seeking to be rid off an obligation in connection with a national insurance scheme; we were claiming that as with the case of old age pensions this parliament should be placed in a position to take it over.
We say that the present government ought immediately to take steps to have the British North America Act amended so as to make possible federal administration so that when the time comes to pay the old age pensions

100 per cent, we shall not be met with any constitutional obstacle to the administration of the scheme in its entirety by the federal government.
That was with regard to old age pensions. I have quoted from Hansard of June 2, 1931, at page 2265. On the same date, at page 2266, I am quoted as follows:
... I say the British North America Act should be amended so as to make it possible for the federal government to undertake the administration of that scheme.
That was the old age pensions scheme. If the act had been amended in that regard an amendment could have been secured easily with regard to unemployment insurance as well.
. . . the time has come when the federal parliament should seek to have the British North America Act amended so as to make it quite clear that it will be within the jurisdiction of this parliament to administer an old age pension act . . .
That was as long ago as 1931; that had been stated before, and I have stated it continually since. On November 22, 1932, I dealt with the same matter again, namely, an amendment of the act but specifically in relation to unemployment insurance. Here are my words, as reported in Hansard of November 22, 1932, at pages 1458 and 1461:
We have always recognized that, if there was to be a national scheme of unemployment insurance, or a national scheme to deal with any phase of social insurance, it would have to be by agreement between the provinces and the dominion, or possibly by an amendment to the British North America Act which could be made as a result of such agreement. Taking that view, we advocated two years and more ago that the government should then and there appoint a commission to deal with the question of unemployment and kindred matters, so that once the necessary data had been secured as a guide to the measure to be drafted, whatever steps might be necessary in the way of an amendment to the British North America Act in order to permit a national scheme of insurance to go into effect could be taken at the earliest possible moment.
At that time, from something the Prime Minister had said, I thought he was going to come round in favour of a national scheme, but apparently he then had something else in mind, evidently what he is attempting to do to-day. In my innocence I took him as meaning he was going on at once with a national unemployment insurance scheme, and said:
We shall I trust be able to work in harmony and cooperation with them. We commend them for their action, but at the same time, we cannot but regret that so long a period has

There was an acceptance of what at that moment seemed to be the intention of the government, to introduce an unemployment insurance measure, but one that it would be within the competence of this parliament to enact.
I have referred at different times to the formal statement of Liberal policy with respect to different matters; the position of the Liberal party in regard to some present day problems, which I made in this house on February 27, 1933, and which sets forth the Liberal policy with respect to these questions of unemployment and unemployment insurance. I will place this statement of policy on record again, so that there can be no question in the mind of anyone as to where we all stand on the matter of unemployment insurance:
Unemployment of First Concern
The Liberal party believes unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem. It would deal with the present emergency conditions through a representative national commission, which would cooperate with the provinces and municipalities in the administration of unemployment relief and in an endeavour to provide work for the unemployed.
As permanent measures the Liberal party is pledged to introduce policies which will serve to provide employment by reviving industry and trade; and to introduce a national system of unemployment insurance.
That is our position. Let me conclude, Mr. Speaker, by pointing out what has been the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite towards that position. I think I have made it very clear that all through this parliament we have been urging-and we started to carry out our endeavour in a preceding parliament-that there should be a national system of unemployment insurance. But every time we have discussed that matter we have been met by objections from hon. gentlemen opposite, and there has been no one whose objections have been stronger and more emphatic than those of the Prime Minister. Let me read what the Prime Minister said about the power of this parliament to deal with this matter and why nothing had been done up to that time, further, why nothing could be done, in view of what the Prime Minister said. I quote from Hansard for November 22, 1932, at page 1452, with regard to unemployment insurance. At that time the Prime Minister referred to what he had said in 1931. I will refer to 1931 a moment later, but I am taking 1932 because he emphasized
his position then in no uncertain terms. Here is what the Prime Minister is reported to have said:
It will be within the memory of most hon. members that on the 29th of April, 1931, I marie a statement with respect to the question of unemployment. In the course of that statement I discussed at some length the question of unemployment or of social insurance that might become the subject matter of legislation to deal with the question of unemployment and allied problems. I pointed out why the government of Canada could not introduce legislation to deal with that matter. Roughly the reasons are two. One is purely a constitutional or legal reason; the other is an economic reason because of lack of information with respect to the subject matter then under discussion.
Can anything be more definite than that? The government, the right hon. gentleman intimated, could not proceed with an unemployment insurance scheme for two reasons. One reason was the economic one of not having the information. I think they were to blame for not having it, but we will let that pass for the moment. The other was the purely constitutional or legal reason which the Prime Minister urged then, had urged before and kept urging at every subsequent session. Further he said:

There, Mr. Speaker, I think is the full explanation of why we have this measure brought down at the present time.
May I say to the Prime Minister that he knows better than anyone else that the final authority that settles these questions of jurisdiction is the courts, and that he cannot by assertion or by assumption give to this parliament any power to deal with these matters ffhich it does not now possess. That is the reason, and the sole reason, why hon. members on this side bring to the attention of the government, as is their duty, and why as leader of the opposition as is my duty I stress the point, that we believe, proceeding as he is, he has adopted a course which will not commend itself to the courts when this legislation comes eventually before them for final decision. In order that I may do the Prime Minister full justice in the matter of the importance he attaches to the judiciary with respect to the interpretation and effect of all legislation, I want to read his words which I have before quoted indirectly, and which I quote directly now. He was speaking at Toronto on February 18, 1932, on the occasion of being called to the bar of Ontario and being made a bencher of the Law Society of Upper Canada. I quote from the Ottawa Journal of February 19, 1932:
Marking centenary celebrations of Osgoode Hall, home of the law courts of the piovince, was the induction of the Prime Minister of Canada as a barrister at law of Ontario.
"I think the judicial branch of government is the most important," said Mr. Bennett, addressing the convocation of benchers of the Law Society after he had been introduced by W. N. Tilley, K.C., treasurer of the Law Society, and sworn in by Clarence Bell, assistant registrar.
"The legislative branch is very important, the executive tremendously so, but in the final analysis the judicial branch of the government is the one to which most attention should be paid. It interprets the acts of the legislative and executive branches, and upon the collective judgment of those we appoint for this purpose depends not only life, liberty and freedom, but the enjoyment of property and all that is thereby involved."
Mr. Speaker, this legislation most certainly will eventually come before the courts for decision. I should like to have seen an unemployment measure passed by this house in accordance with the recommendations of the standing committee on industrial and international relations, a course that would have made the legislation unanimous and would have removed all possibility of doubt as to its validity. When this legislation is passed, there will still be the doubt as to whether it has any validity at all.
[Mr. Bennett.1
In the circumstances, I say to the Prime Minister that in these days of stress and anxiety and suffering for the mass of the people, they are crying for bread and he is giving them a stone. They are crying for fish and he is giving them a serpent; because in addition to their distress and their suffering, when this legislation is found to be ultra vires there will be the sting of bitter disappointment.

Mr. G. G. COOTE (Macleod) moved the second reading of Bill No. 11, to amend the Interest Act.
He said: The principle of this bill is to place in the Interest Act a maximum rate which may be charged or collected on any agreement. The present Interest Act, being chapter 102 of the Revised Statutes of 1927, provides:
Except as otherwise provided by this or by any other act of the parliament of Canada, any person may stipulate for, allow and exact, on any contract or agreement whatsoever, any rate of interest or discount which is agreed upon.
It is these particular words to which I take exception, "any rate of interest which may be agreed upon." The Money Lenders Act, which applies of course to persons engaged in the lending of money, fixes a maximum of twelve per cent as the rate that may be charged; and in the Bank Act there is set a maximum rate of seven per cent that may be charged by the banks. The Interest Act sets no limit. Why place a limit on the rate that may be charged by money lenders but set no maximum rate which may be charged by others? I think we all agree that our experience shows the advisability of placing a limit on the rate that may be charged by money lenders as well as by banks, and I feel it is just as necessary to place a limit on the rate which other persons may collect.
If a limit should be set, what should that limit be? If the banks are limited to seven per cent I can see no reason at the moment why that same rate should not be set for those engaged in general business. Therefore I have drawn this bill, the new section 2 of which fixes a limit of seven per cent. It is a common practice, in western Canada at any rate, to charge rates as high as eight, ten and even twelve per cent per annum. I know that thousands of machine company notes have

Interest Act-Mr. Coote
been drawn carrying a rate of eight per cent until due and ten or even twelve per cent per annum after they are due. Millions of dollars have been paid in interest at these rates, but that is impossible now, with prices as they are. There are millions of dollars owing by retailers to wholesalers, which have been carried on their books for years at the rate of eight per cent, and in many instances the interest is made up and compounded every three months and a draft issued on the retailer. In some instances retailers have told me that they calculate they are paying at least nine per cent per annum in this way, and a general limitation of seven per cent such as I suggest would afford considerable relief to such people. And now that the banks are limited to a rate of seven per cent chargeable to wholesalers, I think this provision I suggest is a very necessary one. Section 3 of the present act provides that when interest is payable on any contract, sale or agreement, and no rate is specified, the rate shall be fixed at five per cent. The new section 3, provides that the rate shall be four per cent. I have proposed that change because it see-ms to me that at the present time all rates should be lower. In section 4 the rate is reduced from five per cent to four per cent. This is where	the	rate of interest is	notannual but is fixed weekly or monthly. A new subsection 5 (a) in the bill fixes a rate of four per cent which may be collected on any mortgage on real estate or any agreement for sale of real estate. I have suggested a rate of four per cent because I believe that the general opinion in this house, as expressed in the debate	last	week,	is that four	percent is probably the maximum which farmers can pay. Certain members however have suggested that	this	is too	low a rate	andthat if it were	fixed	at five	per cent I should
probably get more support for the bill. I may say frankly that it is the principle of establishing a maximum which I am asking for, and if the bill is allowed to have second reading I will move that it be sent to the banking and commerce committee, if that is the wish of the house, and the rate can be decided there. I hope we shall be able to do that.
I do not want to take up too much time, but I feel I should advance a few facts in support of my contention that the rate on real estate mortgages should be lower than it is at the present time and that a maximum should be fixed. So far there has been no limit, and there are to-day some mortgages outstanding at ten per cent, many more at nine per cent, and the bulk in the west at eight per cent. Though in the past many 92582-4Si
farmers have paid off mortgages bearing such rates of interest, that cannot be done to-day. The farmer pays interest out of the products of his farm. In olden times, I believe, he could pay in corn, wine, oil and cattle, but to-day he promises to pay in money and he has no way of monetizing his products; that is done by someone else. To-day, on the average, it takes fifty per cent more of his products to pay his interest than it did at the time he contracted the debt. Further, the farmer can pay only out of his surplus revenue. There are expenditures which he must meet if he is to continue farming, and it might not be out of place to bring before the house a few facts to illustrate the farmer's ability to pay.
Taking the average price of field crop commodities in 1926, the index figure being then 100, we find that in 1930 the index was 57-8; in 1931 it was 46-9; in 1932 it was 43-1; in 1933 it was 52-7, the average for these years being a little less than fifty per cent of their value in 1926. In 1933 the gross value of farm products was only forty-three per cent of what it was in 1928, and by 1933 the average farm income, which had stood at 81,600 in 1928, had fallen to $640. This is the average farm income, and probably half the farms in Canada had a lower income than that shown by the average.
Let me give two or three figures to illustrate the ability of industry to pay interest rates compared to its ability in 1929. In 1929 the gross value of production of the manufacturing industries was $4,029,000,000, and this had fallen in 1933 to $2,086,000,000. I am told that when we speak in terms of millions in this house it goes over the heads of the people; they do not realize what millions mean, but this is another way of stating that for each $1,000 which the manufacturer had for the value of his product in 1929, he had only $500 in 1933. His ability to pay interest had been much more than cut in two. The total amount of wages and salaries paid in the manufacturing industries in 1929 was $813,000,000 and that had fallen to $465,000,000 in 1933. Perhaps I have said enough to indicate that neither the agricultural nor the manufacturing industry can continue to pay rates of interest such as they have done in the past.
There has been a steady depreciation in the money value of all commodities and at the same time for the past five years there has been a steady appreciation of the monetary unit. The holder of money or fixed income bearing securities has found his purchasing power or real income in some cases doubled
Interest Act-Mr. Coote

and in nearly all cases increased by thirty or forty per cent. This has created a grave injustice to debtors; payment in many cases has become impossible and this has resulted in what in olden days would be described as usury. I quote from Mr. Woodlock writing in the Wall Street Journal. He says:
Stated in its simplest form, the prohibition of usury in the middle ages extended to all loans at interest, the use of which did not produce a profit sufficient at least to meet the interest demanded for the loan, or in which the risk or sacrifice on the lender's part was not such as to require legitimate compensation. Probable profit to the borrower, or loss to the lender, justified interest; otherwise in detail that was the rule respecting usury.
If we view the matter in this light, it seems to me that a large part of our debt to-day is usurious and interest thereon has become usury. If the debt cannot be written down, some relief can be given to the debtor by reducing the rate of interest. The country's economy is built on a credit structure. It is quite evident that the structure can be preserved only if the creditor class will make some sacrifice. As Mr. Woodlock says:
It is surely historically true that loans which do not produce the means for repayment are in the long run not repaid'.
And high rate's of interest in the long run are not in the true interest of even the lender.
I would like to give just this one further quotation from Mr. Woodlock. He says:
In the historical perspective of business and industry, when all mistakes have been taken into account and all the changes in the methods and plants duly authorized, it becomes very clear that nature in fact will pay but a very small rate of interest on money-capital, if indeed, in the final book-keeping, she will pay any interest at all.
Two questions are involved in regard to mortgages, that is mortgages already existing and those that may be entered into in the future. I believe the bill as drawn, would refer to both classes and personally I am more concerned with mortgages that are already in existence than with those that may be entered into in the future. I realize the question of federal jurisdiction may be raised in regard to this and I think it is only fair to have the bill go to the committee where that question as well as others relating to the bill may be threshed out.
In conclusion I would just like to say that the principle of the bill as I have introduced it is to establish a maximum rate of interest. It may 'be, as I have said, it is too low; it may be it is too high, but I would just like to say again that if the house would be good

enough to give this bill its second reading and allow it to go to the banking committee

Mr. Speaker, before the minister replies acceding to the request of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), may I be permitted to say a few words in support of the principle embodied 'in this bill. I say the

principle advisedly, because I wholly concur in the suggestion of the hon. member that this bill be sent to the committee on banking and commerce, where, if the principle itself is accepted, the actual rates of interest might be determined.
That principle as I see it is of a dual character; that this parliament should where possible impose a maximum rate of interest which may be charged, and that that rate shall be such as to bear some relation to the ability of the borrowers to pay and to conditions as at present they exist in this country. I think it will be accepted as a fact by all that interest rates are in process of reduction, and that that lowering has become manifest in the sale of government bonds, the interest paid to bank depositors, and in other ways. But there is one point which I should like to stress for a moment; it was brought forward and fully developed in the work of the committee two years ago, which went extensively into the question of debt and interest. During what we usually term normal times, that is times of prosperity-I am speaking of them as normal times for the purpose of argument-I think it will be found that the various divisions of the individual and national income are about equal; that is a certain proportion will go to management, a certain proportion to labour, a certain proportion to invested capital. So long as those various parts hold a reasonable balance one with another, and each absorbs only a fair proportion of the individual and national income, so long the machine will run without undue vibration. But at the present time the situation reminds me somewhat of that form of internal combustion engine which derives its steadiness and power from the smooth running of a very heavy fly wheel. Most of us have seen that form of engine. As long as the wheel is in balance and each section corresponds in weight to the other sections the engine will run and perform its functions and not be subject to undue wear and tear. But if for a moment we try the experiment of overloading one section of that wheel until it weighs twice as much as the other sections, only one result can be expected; the wheel, the engine and the building in which it is situated would be scattered to the four winds and with it the unfortunate men who were attempting to carry on its operation. So far as I can see, Mr. Speaker, our situation is somewhat similar to that unbalanced wheel. The income of the nation and of the individual has been greatly lessened, perhaps by half, but that proportion of it which is expended in the payment of
[Mr. Speakman. 1
capital charges remains much as it was before, and is completely out of balance with all the other factors. It now bears no relationship whatever to the amount of the income which goes in other channels, and to my mind the system in which that is revolving is in the same danger as an internal combustion engine would be if its wheel was off balance.
I believe not only that it is fair but that it is sound economically that the principle of this bill should be accepted. It has been argued that in certain loans and certain forms of lending a higher rate of interest should be charged because of the risks involved, yet I would point out that the element which, above all others, increases the risk of a loan is the charging of a higher rate of interest than the invested money can earn. That is what makes a loan risky; that is what makes repayment doubtful or impossible, and because of that principle I believe the acceptance of this bill, with the determination so far as it is within our power and jurisdiction of the maximum rates which might be charged under those conditions, would be a sound move and one which would be of great assistance to those in debt as well as a stabilizing factor in society itself.
I should like to say just a word about those who are in debt. I remember once attending a meeting of some of the financial fraternity, and :I listened with great interest as they propounded two theories, and I call them theories advisedly. One was that the investor was a public benefactor; eveiyone within hearing and everyone who might read those addresses was urged to save up money and invest it, because in investment lay the strength and life of the nation. But on the other hand they were urged never on any account to go into debt, because debt was something abhorrent and an outrage to nature. I wondered in my inner mind at that time whether they really grasped the significance of this fact, that the two are the same thing viewed from opposite sides, and that you cannot have investment without debt. Not one dollar could be invested unless someone in some way was prepared to go in debt to the amount of that dollar. So the debtor is just as necessary a part of our civilization as is the investor; neither could function without the other. That being the case, and if both are equally important and equally essential, I believe the state should make it a business to see that there should be fair play and fair dealing as -between those two classes.

Interest Act-Mr. Euler
I strongly support the principle of the bill for another reason. We in this corner of the house have been urged again and again from both sides to abandon some of our visionary ideas and take note of the realities of life.
I know of nothing more real, more drastic, more pressing and more demanding of immediate solution than the reality of interest payments upon debt. So in dealing with that question I believe we are dealing in a very practical way with one of the most important realities of life as we face it at the present time. I hope and trust, therefore, and in fact I have every confidence, that the minister will accept this suggestion, permit the bill to receive second reading and then have it sent to the committee on banking and commerce, where its details may be discussed, its scope considered and its application tried out.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a word in connection with this bill because I am very largely in sympathy with the objects that are proposed to be served by it, and more particularly because in at least one of its clauses, that with regard to the proposal to reduce interest on mortgages, it applies to one class of people who have not received a great deal of consideration in this parliament during the last few sessions.
I am not prepared to say whether the rates proposed in the bill, reducing the interest on mortgages to four per cent, should be made retroactive or whether we should enter upon repudiation; I am not much in favour of repudiation. During the last week we discussed in this house a bill intended to relieve the farmers, and particularly the farmers of western Canada. We have had our friends in the corner, as well as hon. members in other parts of the house, year in and year out making a plea on behalf of the farmers, particularly of western Canada and I have no objection at all in that regard. Just a few days ago, in a bill that was before the house, an appropriation of something like 890,000,000 was proposed in order to help the farmers of Canada. I have no particular objection to that, although I am beginning to be a bit apprehensive as to just where we are going to find the money for this particular bill and also for the reform measures which have been proposed by the government. In passing I may say that with regard to unemployment insurance, as with regard to the other measures, one of the vital points to be considered and one of the matters in connection with which I think the house should be taken into the confidence of the government, is just how these moneys are to be raised.
It goes almost without saying-and in this I am suppported by what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) said the other day- that of the 890,000,000 which is to be appropriated a fairly large sum will be lost so far as the country is concerned, and the federal treasury will have to shoulder the burden.

Of late years, with the unemployment that has come to our artisans-and most of our people are employed in industrial establishments-it has become utterly impossible for these men to pay not only the debt instalments on their mortgages but even the interest and the taxes. speechtext:
Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Albemi) moved the second reading of Bill No. 12, to amend the Railway Act (traffic by water).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill is a very simple one, and is almost self explanatory. It is customary for those who oppose a bill to allege that there is lack of precedent for it. However in the present instance I can point to precedents which have run back for twenty-nine years. Section 358 of the Railway Act reads as follows:
The provisions of this act shall, in respect of tolls, tariffs and joint tariffs, so far as deemed applicable by the board, extend and apply to the traffic carried by any railway company by sea or by inland water, between any ports or places in Canada, if the company owns, charters, uses, maintains or works, or is a party to any arrangement for using, maintaining or working vessels for carrying traffic by sea or by inland water between any such ports or places.
I would emphasize the fact that that section has been in existence for twenty-nine years, but has no relation whatever and conveys no

suggestion of its being applicable only to through traffic, carried so far by land and so far by water. It is entirely applicable to carriage by water alone. I might best explain the bill by saying that its provisions are the same as those in the section I have just read, except that I would leave out the word "railway" and the expression '"by inland sea", the idea being ,to make it apply to any company owning vessels and carrying traffic, either passengers or freight, by sea. I do however desire one or two slight changes which should be given in detail.
In the first place I make the section apply to vessels other than those owned by a railway company. In other words I make it apply to all vessels carrying freight and passengers by sea. Although I do not include the great lakes, I have no objection to the section applying to the great lakes, if the committee to which the bill may be referred to desires. However, I am not familiar with the conditions on the great lakes, and I do not wish to raise issues about which I do not know. I make it apply merely to coastal waters of both coasts. I ask that the routes and points of call should be supervised in exactly the same way, and by the same body as is now done under the board of railway commissioners in connection with the points of call and routes of railways. I also make an exception of boats under twenty tons burthen, so as not to require that small ferries should come under the restrictions or conditions of the provision.
Apart from that the section would apply to all vessels, the system which now applies to all vessels owned by a railway. If it is right and proper that it should apply to vessels owned by a railway I cannot see why it should not apply to another company which may probably or possibly be competing with a railway company, but which does not happen to own a railway. I believe the provision would be beneficial to all parties concerned. Communities served by the boats in question which may believe they have been overlooked or are not receiving the service to which they are entitled, or the rates they would like to have, could apply to the board of railway commissioners. On the other hand there is distinct and absolute protection for a shipping company from, we will say, political pressure. Perhaps some member of parliament may want a particular coastal boat to call at his summer home or that of his friends, and for that reason exerts the pressure necessary to have that done. Perhaps directly or indirectly the hint is thrown out that if the suggestion is

not complied with there may be difficulty in having a subsidy renewed. That would not be a desirable condition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter came up in the house ten years ago. Railways and the telephone
and express companies are subject to regulation by a board created by this parliament known as the board of railway commissioners, and I see no reason why shipping companies engaged in the great lakes and also in the coastal trade should not be subject to regulation in the same way. I was chairman of the Toronto harbour board for a great many years when the waterfront and harbour development was going on in Toronto, and I know something of the labour conditions on the vessels that ply out of that port and on the great lakes. The labour conditions are an absolute disgrace to the people of this country. Men are working on those boats night and day until the fall of the year bringing down the grain on its way from the west to the seaboard, and there are not adequate life saving facilities and life saving stations. As I said in this house in the sessions of 1922 and 1923 these vessels crossing lake Superior have to depend on an American wireless station, and almost every year there are disasters on the great lakes. Such conditions would not foe permitted in any other line of business. Manufacturers, for instance, cannot work their men the way these men are worked on these boats on the great lakes. I do not wish to be harsh in my criticism because I know that shipping is in a precarious state, but I have seen men going out on these ships under conditions that defy all the known laws of hygiene, away down in the bottom of the hold of a vessel twenty or thirty or forty years old, and at night it is worse than the black hole of Calcutta. The health officer of Toronto complained to me about conditions on these ships twelve years ago when I was chairman of the harbour commission. I think that the principle of this bill should foe considered by parliament because labour conditions on the vessels on the great lakes demand reform at the hands of this parliament. I would not take the responsibility of defeating this bill by talking it out. I am supporting the principle of proper labour conditions on the vessels on the great lakes, and I would like to see the principle of this bill considered by a committee of this house with a view to action being taken by parliament.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister) for the second reading of Bill No. 8, to establish an employment and social insurance commission, to provide for a national employment service, for insurance against unemployment, for aid to unemployed persons, and for other forms of social insurance and security, and for purposes related thereto.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at six o'clock the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) had just finished a lengthy address on the bill now before the house. If I may say so, his speech was divided into two parts, the first dealing with the constitution and the constitutional difficulties standing in the way of the enactment of this legislation, and the second giving a sort of resume of the activities and efforts of the Liberal party in regard to social legislation between the years 1919 and 1930. The right hon. gentleman laid particular stress on the Old Age Pensions Act that was passed under the Liberal administration. The greater part of his remarks had very little reference to the bill now before the house. I do not wish to follow him in all that he said, but I would like to make one or two observations with respect to some of the matters dealt with in his address.
The right hon. gentleman laid much stress on the constitutional difficulties and the rights of the provinces, but very little stress on the rights of the federal parliament. After all, if this parliament or the provincial legislatures all took the attitude that they were going to stand by the very letter of their rights under the British North America Act, then government in this country would become almost an impossibility. I believe that the members of this house as well as the members of the provincial legislatures ought to take a broad view of the situation as it exists in Canada; for if we are to take a narrow view then progressive legislation will become almost impossible. In the past few years this government, as governments previously have done, has assisted the provinces in the matter of unemployment, and if the federal parliament

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Heaps
took the stand that the question of unemployment was entirely one for the provinces, then the provinces to-day would indeed be in a very bad position. However, since this bill has been introduced I know of no province which so far has taken any objection to it; in fact, I know of a number of provinces that have hailed with a good deal of satisfaction the introduction of an unemployment insurance bill in the House of Commons.
This afternoon the leader of the opposition, in discussing this measure, hinted at the rights of the provinces with particular reference to Ontario, and he indicated that that province was at the present time investigating its own rights in regard to certain taxation which the federal government was levying there. That sounded rather strange to me, for I read in this morning's paper that the Premier of Ontario had used the following language-it is to be found in a Canadian Press dispatch:
There won't be work unless the federal government assist us. . . . We are not able to do it
ourselves.
That is rather strange, I say, coming from a government who, it is claimed, will stand entirely upon their provincial rights. Then we were told something about the legal obstacles that stand in the way. Unfortunately we are compelled to leave these legal difficulties in the hands of the lawyers, and I presume we must allow them to fight the matter out.
Another objection raised by the leader of the Liberal party to this legislation was the fact that the provincial governments had not been consulted in the matter. I wondered whether, when the old age pensions legislation was passed in 1926, the provincial governments had been consulted in that regard.
