provincial governments had a responsibility under that act. whereas under this bill they
have no responsibility. Under this legislation the provincial governments will be relieved of certain responsibilities, whereas under that act they were asked to assume heavy obligations. But the party in power at that time introduced the legislation without consulting the provinces, just as the present government has done in connection with this bill. I cannot see therefore that the argument of the present leader of the opposition has very much to commend it when he urges that the government should have consulted the provinces before introducing this legislation.
The leader of the opposition also complained about the Senate having thrown out the old age pension bill in 1926. It is quite true that the Conservative majority in the Senate threw out that measure in 1926, but I notice that only twenty-one members voted in favour of the bill, one of whom I believe was a Conservative. There were more than twenty Liberal members in the Senate in
1926.	Where did the others disappear to when the vote was taken?
If I wanted to go back into the dim and distant past to look up what had been said by one party or the other I could find a great deal to be said against both parties. I remember that in 1927 when a motion was introduced in this house to have submitted to a committee the question of unemployment insurance we heard language which does not now commend itself to those who used it on that occasion, such as this, for instance:
Whosoever becomes the victim of unemployment. in this country, does so because he has no desire to wrork; he really refuses work.
It was one of the Liberal members who said that, when we were discussing the question of unemployment insurance on March 16,
1927,	as will be found at page 1277 of Hansard. Another member said this:
How is it possible to imagine that the government can grant every request of the country -among others tax reduction-and at the same time establish pensions for old' age, the blind, workmen and destitute people over the whole country? I consider it absurd.
I could go on quoting at great length along this line but it serves no useful purpose and I do not intend to do so. It is more the part of true statesmanship to think of the present as well as the future and to deal less with the past. I have no objection to prime ministers and leaders of oppositions, even the opposition in this comer, changing their minds. It denotes at times not only good tactics but sound common sense when,

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Heaps
in view of changed conditions, they are prepared to change their own particular opinion. This afternoon we had a speech from the Prime Minister. Now the Prime Minister is a very able lawyer; in fact, if ever I wanted a lawyer to defend me on some particular charge my first choice would be, in spite of my dislike for lawyers, the present Prime Minister. But the right hon. gentleman made one significant admission which I think is unusual for our Prime Minister. He said that he had other ideas for relieving the unemployment situation. Possibly it was a slip of the tongue; he evidently had something in his mind, and I think myself that before he introduced legislation dealing with unemployment insurance we should have had from him what is after all his remedy for unemployment. It is far more important to deal with the problem of unemployment than with the problem of unemployment insurance, and if the government have any remedy now for the most important problem parliament has to deal with, then I suggest that this is the time for the Prime Minister to give us his ideas in the matter. I do believe that before we start on the question of unemployment insurance we ought to deal first with the fundamental problem of unemployment itself. I submit that it will be almost an impossibility, with things as they are, for us to deal in any comprehensive way with the problem of unemployment insurance.
When the bill was introduced in the resolution stage I claimed that with conditions as we have them now, with the numbers of people who are out of work, it would be almost impossible to have what one might term an actuarially sound system of unemployment insurance that would give relief benefits to even a small number of those who unfortunately find themselves out of work at the present time. The figures submitted by the Prime Minister this afternoon showed that at the time of the census in 1931 there were 2,566,031 people who were employed in that year. He claimed that there were affected by the present bill 1,701,834 persons, the vast majority of whom were male employees. But some rather significant omissions present themselves in those figures given by the Prime Minister this afternoon, for in the census figures of 1931 information as to the number of unemployed was not given. We do not know how many of those approximately two and a half million people are out of work now and we do not know how many of the approximately one and two-thirds millions who, it is claimed, might be affected by the bill, would actually come under its provisions.
[Mr. Heaps.)
I would venture to assert that tremendous reductions would have to be made from the figures given by the Prime Minister this afternoon to indicate exactly or even approximately how many people are affected by the proposed measure.
Since these census figures were taken, our unemployed army has grown to a considerable extent, and further there is in the bill a very important provision which states that those who are casually employed would not become beneficiaries under the proposed legislation. I do not know how they are going to define the term " casual worker." For the past five years numbers of men employed in railway shops have been employed only part of the time. Let me take for instance the Canadian Pacific shops. The men employed in those shops are working and have been working fourteen days a month since, I believe, the end of 1929 or some time in 1930. At fourteen days a month, or less than three and a half days a week, on an average throughout the year those men will not have worked twenty-five hours a week. Under the provisions of the bill would those men be termed casual employees? The chances are that if a legal interpretation were given, they could not be called permanent employees because they are working only three and a half days a week and they might quite possibly come under the category of part time or casual employees. This would almost immediately debar from the operation of the measure a vast number of men employed in both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National shops, for what applies to the Candian Pacific in the number of hours worked applies in almost the same way to the Canadian National shops as well.
I have had protests from some of these railwaymen's organizations in regard to the bill. In fact, so far as the bill itself is concerned, I have had up to now more condemna tion than I have had commendation from the workers in different parts of the dominion, for we find that to a railway employee or to almost every other casual employee, that is one who is employed only part time, this would mean that he is expected to contribute to a scheme of unemployment insurance almost the equivalent of one cent an hour of his wages. I would like to remind the Prime Minister, although he is not in his seat at the moment, that when the resolution was before the house he promised to give us certain information in the form of printed matter, namely a report of Mr. Andrew D. Watson and Mr. Hugh H. Wolfenden, actuaries, who worked on this bill for quite a considerable length of time. I think he promised hon. members that

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Heaps
the printed report of those two gentlemen *would be available before the second reading of the bill was taken up. Personally I was waiting for the submission of that document in order that I might have a better idea of the conclusion those gentlemen had arrived at .and the reasons for certain financial provisions of the bill.
Reference was made this afternoon to the .act in Great Britain, the statement being made to the house and the impression probably being given to the country that the proposed legislation to a very large extent followed the act as they have it in the old country. To a certain extent that may be true, but it is true in only a very limited sense, for in England at the present time the legislation is so all-embracing that it covers, I would say, more than one-quarter of the whole population of that country. In Canada I do not think the provisions of the bill will cover ten per cent of our population; that is, assuming we have 1,000,000 insured- and I do not think that figure will be reached for a great number of years-then only shall we have ten per cent of our population covered as against more than twenty-five per cent under the British act. Further, the unemployment insurance act in Great Britain has a definite purpose in view, which is to provide for men and women who are out of work. In this country our bill does not provide for them at all. We start on a completely different basis; we select a number of insurable risks and all the uninisurable risks are discarded until such time as they become insurable risks. The consequence is that we are going to take the good risks that probably do not require insurance, while the poorer risks that require more insurance than the better ones will have to go without insurance at all.
Moreover, the unemployment insurance act in Great Britain has been widened in its scope over a great number of years until to-day, as I said, it has become so all-embracing that very few men or women in the old country are outside its provisions. In Canada where for a number of years we have had such a huge army of unemployed and semi-employed, these men and women will unfortunately be altogether outside the provisions of the bill. That is brought about because the government intend, as was stated here by the Prime Minister this afternoon, to have an actuarially sound system of unemployment insurance. If we are to have a bill that is worth while we cannot have it actuarially sound, for the simple reason that so many men and women are out of work, there is such a vast army
of unemployed, that substantial contributions from the state, far greater than anything contained in the bill, are required in ordeir to give benefits approaching anything worth -while.
Second, are we likely in the immediate or even the distant future to be able to have a bill that will include within its scope the numbers of men and women actually engaged in industry in this dominion? I remember the first session I came to this house one of the questions I raised was that of unemployment insurance, -and practically every year until 1931 without exception I brought that matter up on the floor of this house-advocating some form of unemployment insurance to cope with the problem that was then confronting us. But from the year 1931 on I have not been half so enthusiastic for unemployment insurance as I was prior to that time; not because I did not want provision to be made for the unemployed-quite the opposite-but because I believe that if we are to attack the problem of unemployment successfully we have to attack it from an entirely different angle than mere unemployment insurance. Again, if we are to have a scheme of insurance that will take care of the unemployed, the numbers of unemployed in Canada will have to be reduced very greatly in order that the scheme may be actuarially feasible.
Why do I say I am not so enthusiastic today for such a measure as I was a few years ago? In 1927, 1928 and 1929 I introduced motions in this house, feeling that some form of insurance might be introduced that would take care of the problem in some effective way. In 1931 the Prime Minister was good enough to accept the motion. He stated that during the lifetime of this parliament a bill would be introduced dealing with the question. I have no doubt that it is pursuant to that pledge that we have this bill before us to-day. But when I advocated unemployment insurance in this house the number of unemployed was small compared with the number we have at this time. I was not as wise as some other people; I thought that the depression which struck us in 1929 and continued through 1930 and 1931 would pass away as other depressions have, and that we should again enter a cycle of better times, when the number of unemployed would be reduced. But the depression continued; the army of unemployed has grown larger, and to-day I venture to say that in this country it numbers approximately 600,000 people, in spite of the figures given by the Prime Minister. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler)
"66	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Heaps
mentioned this afternoon the vast number of men and women on relief in Kitchener. I was told that in Toronto there are now more people on relief than there ever have been, that the number has reached a peak, more being on relief this year than last. With such a great number of people on relief I cannot understand how we can still claim that the number of unemployed has been cut in half since 1932. However, as I say I thought that the acute condition that prevailed in 1929 and 1930 would abate. Such has not been the case; we still have to-day what some refer to as an abnormal condition. I am wondering whether such conditions have not really become normal; for in addition to the vast numbers who are completely out of work we have other vast numbers working only part time, yet the industrial machine is running n the regular manner. So if the present conditions, these so-called abnormal conditions, are really more or less normal, then we must attack the problem from an entirely different angle.
Last year I brought in a resolution on the question of shorter hours and increased purchasing power for the masses of ithe people, and again I was thankful when the government accepted the motion and it passed the house unanimously. But I was very much disappointed when probably as a result of that resolution a bill was brought in ithis year for a forty-eight hour working week. If that is the beet the government can do I am afraid that the lot of the unemployed is not going to be helped. In fact our army of unemployed is going ,to become a permanent thing in this country. I should like to see an attempt made to deal with the question in, a far more radical and fundamental way than anything proposed by the government up to the present time.
As far as this bill is concerned it demands from the employer and the employee a contribution of twenty-five cents a week, while the government is to assume probably from 10 to 22J cents as its share. No doubt this arrangement is somewhat similar to what prevails in other countries, and the benefits proposed somewhat similar to those given in other countries. But in other countries unemployment insurance was introduced a good many years ago, and we are beginning now on an extremely limited scale. I think we should look at this bill in a cold, logical way to see what it really will do.
In the first place I think it is generally admitted that as far as unemployment is concerned it does not begin to touch the question at all. It merely attempts to form a fund out

of which benefits could be paid, and we are not sure as to the amount of those benefits, for the Prime Minister told us this afternoon very distinctly that a committee or commission would be set up to administer the act and that the benefits given might vary from time to time according to the actuarial condition of the fund. For instance at a time when a large number of the insured were unemployed the benefits to be paid might be less than those now set out in the bill. At the present time those out of work do receive certain relief. Responsibility for that rests upon the federal and provincial governments and the municipalities, each contributing about one-third. I venture to say that in a general way the amount of relief granted to persons out of work is about equivalent to the benefits proposed to be given under this bill. If such be the case, what does it mean? It means that what is now a responsibility of the province, the municipality and the federal government is to become a responsibility of the federal government, the employer and the employee; and those who subsequently find themselves in the ranks of the unemployed and who come under the provisions of the bill will not be taken care of by the provincial and municipal administrations. In other words the share now borne by the province and the municipality is to be loaded upon the employer and the employee.
I have said that I have no objection to the principle of unemployment insurance. I did hope, however, that when a bill was introduced the government would have been far more generous, and actually in some way undertake to care for the unemployed in Canada. I know it might be rather a tall order to ask the government to take care of the unemployed men and women at the present time; nevertheless they have to be taken care of in some way, and when we are offered a bill which will have the effect of taking out the good risks and leaving the bad ones to take care of themselves as best they can, we are doing a great injustice to a large proportion of the men and women who still hope to be employed in industry at some time in the future if not now.
Parliament has not, and could not have, any greater responsibility than that of dealing with the problem of unemployment, and whether or not I like it I have to compare the bills now before the house with the impression created throughout the country by the radio speeches of the Prime Minister. I heard those speeches and read them in the press, and when the newspapers asked me what I thought of these new ideas, this new

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Stanley
deal or whatever you may call it, I was one of the first to say that I congratulated the Prime Minister on his conversion. The only reservation I made in giving my congratulations was that I wanted to see the measures themselves when they came before the house.
I must confess to a certain amount of disappointment in both the present bill and the measure concerning hours of labour. The people of this country expected something more and something better from the government than is contained in either of these measures. You cannot place measures of this kind before the workers of this country and make them believe that they will improve their standard or help their lot in life; after all what the average person wants is a feeling of security, and neither the forty-eight hour week measure nor this unemployment insurance bill will give them any more security than they have at the present time. As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, what I expect from this or any government is that they will get down to fundamentals in dealing with the problem confronting them, and which is likely to confront any government even after another election. We want to see them deal with the problem of unemployment, not only by means of an unemployment insurance bill but also in a more fundamental way than is expressed in the terms of this measure. I expect that about three-quarters of a million people will come under the provisions of this bill, and those men and women will be the people who least require this sort of insurance, for if a person is employed at the present time, under present depressed conditions, he is not likely to be out of work one or two years hence. So I think in this parliament we should have before us those other ideas at which the Prime Minister hinted this afternoon, in dealing with the problem of unemployment.
I confess openly, Mr. Speaker, with regard to this unemployment insurance bill, that it is hardly wanted by those who favoured it and is not wanted by those who opposed it. It is so negligible in the benefit it is to give the working people of the country that I think we will disappoint a great many of them, and I feel that it is almost an injustice to pass this measure unless its scope is made much wider than is the case at present. Perhaps before the bill is through the house the Prime Minister and the government may be in a more generous mood; perhaps the provisions of the act may be widened and the government may make larger grants than have been suggested up to the present. I do
not want to be too harsh in my criticism;
I would far rather be able to stand up and say to the government, "Thank you for what you have done in providing a measure that will be worth while," but a measure of this kind, so limited in scope and in the benefit it is to give, I am afraid will not be received with much enthusiasm by the working people of Canada.
As I have said already, Mr. Speaker, the problem of unemployment is more important than the question of unemployment insurance. I would far rather have heard from the government the proposals they have in mind to deal with the question of unemployment; then, assuming that their proposals could not entirely absorb those who are out of work, an unemployment insurance bill might be a valuable addition to their program, because it might take care of the limited number of unemployed. A program of public works is not a cure for unemployment; desirable though it may be to tide over a temporary situation, it cannot be regarded as a permanent cure. So I hope that before the bill receives third reading we may have from the government a further declaration as to what they intend to do to meet the unemployment situation in this country and what they intend to do for the army of unemployed who cannot now and probably never will be able to become absorbed into the industrial life of this country. Perhaps if they do submit to the house something worth while we might be able to feel a little more enthusiastic about this unemployment insurance measure than I feel at the present time.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with curious interest to the address of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). There can be no argument against the government dealing with unemployment as best it can; there can be no argument against the obligation which the people of Canada owe to those unemployed in industry, but I cannot understand or justify the hon. gentleman and othen who confuse the consideration of the questioi of unemployment insurance with the questioi of granting relief to those who cannot receive benefits under such an insurance scheme.
The problem of unemployment is unquestionably a problem which belongs to industry as a whole, and in that I include the obligation which the governments of our country owe because of their association with industry. Unquestionably the hon. gentleman is quite correct when he asserts that unemployment is not the result of choice on the
768	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Stanley
part of the workman himself. Nor are those right who assume or imply, speaking in general, that the people who are unemployed are in that position because of a lack of energy or prudence or because of laziness on their part. That, of course, is the absurd argument we hear at times. The fact of the matter is that there is a distinct weakness in *the system of industry as it has been carried on in this and other countries in that it has aot provided for the continuous or steady employment of workmen associated with industry. The hon. gentleman would indicate that we must deal with relief on the one hand or with insurance on the other, and that the presentation to this parliament of a bill to deal with unemployment insurance means that no measures will or can be taken for the relief of the unemployed. Of course that is neither a fair nor a reasonable contention. To my mind there is no reason why tradesmen either within or without the unions should not be able to make their contributions along with others associated in industry who are helping to provide an insurance fund to enable them to carry on their work with reasonable security. The hon. gentleman is quite correct when he states that the workman's greatest need is a reasonable sense of security. The ideal to which he strives is that he may be self-supporting, and by that I mean that during his working years he may be able to earn enough to provide for the maintenance of his family during his whole life. The same should be said regarding industry as a whole; it should be self-supporting in the sense that during the twelve months of the year it will be able to fulfil its obligations to the human element connected with it. There has been a lack of organization which has been more marked in the last four or five years, but which existed even before the depression.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg contrasted what is recommended in Bill No. 8 with measures which have been in operation in the United Kingdom. I shall not discuss the matter in detail, but I will say that there are differences. One does not have to be satisfied that Bill No. 8 includes all the virtues of the legislation in Great Britain in order to conclude that there are virtues in it. We realize that the general principle of the bill before us is the principle which has been followed in the old country for the last thirty years. The details have varied, and improvements have been made there until it reached a point where in 1934 a distinct advance was shown over the legislation which had been in force during preceding years. What has been 
the result in the old country? I do not think anyone would doubt that there has been a distinct change in the psychology of the public in general, and in that I include not only the employees but the employers-industries, governments, trade unions, and the population in general-until to-day, and in fact it has been so for a considerable number of years, we find no real opposition to the principle of insurance. If one were to study the report of the Blanesburgh committee he would find through it expressions of confidence and of approval from all sections of the public. At one point the committee reports:
Nobody has suggested to us that the principle of unemployment insurance should be abandoned. It has been recognized by all who have appeared before us, and we ourselves share the view, that an unemployment insurance scheme must now be regarded' as a permanent feature of our code of legislation.
When we in this chamber undertake to introduce this form of social legislation we are accepting the principle set forth in the report of the Blanesburgh committee. In 1924 the national federation of employers' organizations [DOT]-and I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that it is an association of employers' organizations-set out their approval in the following terms:
Whatever be the defects of the emergency measures, the experiment of compulsory unemployment insurance, as initiated in 1911, cannot be adjudged a failure in itself. On the contrary, experience since 1911 has proved that it is practicable in normal times to make provision. by way of insurance, for assisting the bona fide workman over periods of temporary and unavoidable unemployment.
Then, passing on down one comes to the Melchett-Tumer group which gave its hearty approval to the scheme. Then the Liberal industrial inquiry gave its approval, and again later the Balfour committee appointed by the board of trade expressed the opinion that-
-both from the point of view of general social welfare and from that of industrial and commercial efficiency, establishing of unemployment insurance in Great Britain had been amply justified, adding that they would find it difficult to imagine how the country would have fared "had not the insurance machinery been available in its time of need." Indeed, as they say, it is a subject of constant comment that "so deep and prolonged a trade depression has produced so little actual suffering in comparison with the experience of far slighter and more transient periods of depression before the war," a condition avhich they attribute in large part to the unemployment insurance scheme.
And so we have various bodies representing all sections of the public giving their hearty approval to the general principle. I realize that there may be criticism of the details,

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Stanley
but in Canada we have reached the point where social legislation of the type before us is being demanded by the general public. I have no doubt the trade unions of Canada will approve the principle of contributory insurance as it is contained in Bill No. 8, and I have no doubt they will support the measure despite the endeavour on the part of some to confuse a legitimate insurance scheme with a program of unemployment relief. I believe such insurance in this country is not a form of charity; it is not a gratuity, but it is good business. In my view when we provide for the human element in industry we are just using ordinary, common, everyday business tactics. As it is organized to-day society has reached the point where it recognizes that industry cannot survive unless it is prepared to take its part in bringing about social legislation such as that we are now considering.
If one took the time to review the legislation of the old country, he could go through the various amendments that have been made, showing that they did experiment during the years. For example, during the six years from 1920 to 1926 there were sixteen different enactments changing the application of the insurance principle. I think, however, it is safe to assume that the legislation as they have it now is fairly well fixed and that it is a permanent acquisition to the needs of industry in that great country.
What has been taking place in the old country? What has been changing the psychology of their people? During the last thirty-five years the expenditure on social services in the United Kingdom has increased from $180,000,000 to $2,500,000,000. Even since 1908 the expenditure on social services in the United Kingdom has multiplied five times, and the remarkable feature to my mind is that less than one-eighth of the total amount spent on their social services consists of relief extended under the poor laws or as relief itself.
Much has been said in regal 1 to armaments, and it is very interesting to note this fact. In 1914, just before the war, Great Britain was spending on armaments about $350,000,000 a year, a sum equal to that which she was spending at that time on social services. Last year they were maintaining about the same quantity of armaments, at a cost of $575,000,000, about half as much again, but instead of spending $350,000,000 on social services that expenditure had multiplied to $2,500,000,000. While this was going on in the United Kingdom, showing the change in the attitude of the public towards social services there, France had multiplied her expenditure on armaments by six, Italy by five, Japan by five, and the United States by 92582-49
three. In the United Kingdom when unemployment there was at its worst, in 1929, between two-thirds and three-quarters of the number of those insured were persons who were regularly employed, and the average unemployment amongst the men was 140 days and amongst the women 93 days.
Coming to the bill before the house, as the Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett, pointed out this afternoon, this is an insurance bill. It provides for cash contributions by way of benefits for cash paid in by way of premiums, and that of course is an insurance proposition. Granted that it is insurance on an actuarial basis, I think it should be remembered that the bill goes beyond the matter of insurance pure and simple and provides machinery to give thought and organization to the whole question of unemployment as it is to be related to this insurance scheme.
One of the dangers of unemployment insurance which has been spoken of heretofore is that it may steer employers and employees away from the obligation which they have of organizing themselves to keep employment more regular and continuous. The labour exchanges wdiich are to be set up under this bill are a very important feature in the carrying out of any unemployment insurance scheme. The bill provides for the regular and systematic placement of labour; it provides for the mobility of labour, which industry unquestionably requires; it provides also that the commission shall have authority to investigate, take evidence, and keep in touch with the movement of labour so that the proper measures may from time to time be taken to provide for the mobility of labour and the placing of men where their services are required. That means that thought is being diverted to the proper channels to assist in overcoming the difficulties of unemployment in our country.
I do not assume for a moment that this legislation is to be regarded as a measure for relieving the present emergency of unemployment in this country, but I do say this, that when you have the insurance scheme organized, and when the commission is set up with thought and organization behind it, then beyond the actual contributions provided for in this legislation the scheme will assist by serving as a prophylactic, if I may call it such, as a preventive of unemployment which might otherwise be thrown on the labour market. The scheme as we have it before us not only provides through its insurance facilities for the assistance of the men who are employed, but it provides for that thought and organization of which I

770	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Stanley
have been speaking, and it does help to provide the government and the people of this country with an organized system looking to regular employment, which must undoubtedly be of benefit in the years to come.
May I say one word more in regard to these exchanges, and I do not think this point has yet been brought out except that it has been mentioned that it is necessary for cooperation between the provinces and the commission to be set up under this legislation. To my mind there must also be the utmost cooperation between the workmen on the one hand and the exchanges on the other. There must be on both sides that feeling of confidence, that spirit which will help in coordinating the obligations which belong to the exchanges. That cannot be emphasized too strongly because unless the cooperation be such that the employees on the one hand and the employers on the other have the utmost confidence in the con>-petenoe of the exchanges to perform that task of placing labour, of making it more mobile, then one of the most important features will be defeated.
May I bring up this point, which I think is a refutation of what the hon. member for North Winnipeg has said, that the exchange must be for the placement of labour, not as a detective agency, not as a semi police force, not as an agency for the distribution of relief or for the administration of relief measures. To my mind that should be removed entirely to the proper authorities and organizations; that work does not belong to the exchanges which will be set up under the provisions of this bill.
Further, the bill provides preventive measures. Section 7 (c) provides, practically speaking, for juvenile training, one of the most important features of the bill. It gives power to the commission to take whatever steps it may see fit to attain the knowledge and, having attained the knowledge, to apply it for providing preventive measures, the training of the young men. This is to salvage young people particularly from that part of labour which is most overcrowded. And that part is the unskilled labour. In the old country it is shown that ninety-three per cent of the men who drew their benefits under the insurance act were those who had left school before the age of fourteen. There is food for thought in that little bit of information; and if the provision of the bill gives to the commission the authority to use their intelligence, their conscience, their thought and their organizing ability to train the young to a more profitable form of labour, where 
labour will not be so overcrowded, then it will have done a great work in that line alone.
The bill provides for national health in part 4, which is also of very considerable significance. It is a wise intitial step to be taken before any systematic and really effective measures can be pursued for the further extension of social health insurance.
Beyond the immediate active provisions of this bill, section 7 (a) provides for what has been termed in some of the old country discussions the second line of defence-those who have exhausted their benefits of the insurance scheme. Section 7 not only empowers the commission but it puts upon them the obligation to use their time, their ability and their every opportunity to adopt measures that will assist in meeting this particular form of labour problem comprising those who have exhausted their benefits under the provisions of the bill. Then it goes a step further and gives them the authority to consider the whole question of unemployment. That does not bring the unprovided for unemployed under the benefits of the bill, but it does the very thing which the hon. member for North Wininpeg contended, which is that men who have the opportunity, an official body who have the authority, should give the best consideration to the great question of unemployment in a national way. And the measure so provides.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the other day did suggest that insurance and relief should not be separated. I think that those who have looked into the question of unemployment insurance will take the opposite view, that that is the very thing that should not happen, and that relief should not be grafted on to insurance in any way. If that is done the result will be of course that the employed worker will be contributing to the assistance of the unemployed citizens of the country. In other words, we shall be taxing employment to extend relief to those who unfortunately are on relief in this country. No one contends that nothing should be done for the unemployed. No one contends that the governmental and other agencies should not use their utmost power and thought in meeting that problem. On the other hand, no wise person would suggest that that part of the unemployment distress in this country should be provided for by the contributions which will be made by employed workmen into the insurance fund. That would be at once disastrous to the insurance undertaking; it is one of the things that should not be done. To my mind, this bill should provide, and it does provide for a

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Neill
dignified insurance contract, and that should not be confused with any relief dole or relief contribution. On the one hand we are legislating for insurance, and on the other, when there is suitable legislation, we are providing for relief. But the insurance bill itself cannot be a mongrel measure, mixing up relief for the unemployed who do not come under the insurance scheme with the insurance benefits extended to those who do come under it.
One of the potential virtues of this bill is that the community as a whole will benefit through the sustaining of the purchasing power of our workmen in all the various classifications under the bill, during twelve months of the year, particularly during those months or weeks when it is impossible for a section of them to find work. It also sustains the morale of that part of our industry throughout the length and breadth of our country; it also prompts our employers to employ more labour. But in addition it has its danger, and that is the danger of demoralization. So often we hear of the demoralization of the employees, but there is not very much danger of demoralization of the employees who come under the measure. The greater danger is of demoralizing the employers or the government or the trade unions or those who may by reason of the smooth working of the legislation refuse to give that careful attention, that organization, which should be continued for the proper working of industry throughout the dominion
I listened with considerable interest to the address delivered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon. It was a speech of defence and excuses. I am quite willing to allow him that privilege; I shall endeavour to be magnanimous enough to excuse him for his excuses, but after all one has no particular inclination to discuss political platforms of years gone by. As a matter of fact I do not know very much about, nor am I particularly interested in the platforms of the various parties in years gone by. I am not concerned very much with the professions of political faiths, but as we stand to-day, I am concerned with action translated into legislation on the statute books of our country. That is what the Canadian people are interested in; the justification of former contentions or the glorifying or the condemnation of political platforms of years gone by is of very little interest. I agree heartily with the hon. member for North Winnipeg that we are not interested in those matters and that it is no sin for any politician or statesman to change his mind. I do not know nor do I care whether there have been any changes of mind, so long as to-day, when 92582-491
we are considering the question of unemployment insurance, we get a bill which will extend to the workmen of our country the insurance which they have been seeking.
The leader of the opposition may be quite content with the negative policy which he has presented and which he contended had been in existence for so long in the platform of his party, but I must congratulate the government on its positive policy incorporated in Bill No. 8 now under consideration. I presume the right hon. gentleman for the present is opposed to Bill No. 8; I could gather nothing else from his argument, although he did not so state in so many words. But whether the opposition comes by reason of some constitutional argument or by reason of some other argument in regard to principle, is of no significance in the result; if it means opposition to the legislation, if it means an endeavour to defeat the practical scheme comprised in Bill No. 8, then the right hon. gentleman and his party have done their share to oppose what labour in general in this country has been demanding for many years past.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN EMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The title of the bill promises us a good deal more than does the bill itself, which proposes to enact only two things. One is an extension of the employment offices now in existence and the second is a very limited scheme of unemployment insurance. Dealing first with the employment offices, I anticipate it is the design of the government to extend the existing system. I believe there are sixty-six such offices now. I have no doubt that this will be a good policy; it will cost a good deal of money, but I think it will be worth it. I see one point that might cause trouble. Under section 14 the commission has power to make regulations to make advances by way of loan for the fare of unemployed men to some point where they have secured work, and it states that such advances will be a debt due to the commission and recoverable by process of law. It might well be that that would take the form of a lien on the men's wages and we might have this situation: two hundred men at Vancouver might be sent to the wheat fields in Alberta with a lien on their wages. It would take them at least two months to earn enough money to pay off that lien. They might then be thrown out of work and have no money with which to return to British Columbia. Some provision would have to be made to safeguard against a situation of that kind. But the general principle of that feature of the measure is sound and I will gladly support it.
772	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Neill
The second phase of the bill is the unemployment Insurance. I have advocated this for many years and I must support the bill although I am disappointed at the limited extent of it. I accept the principle of contributions because I have always realized that without contributions it would not be an insurance sy-trm; it would be merely a dole. It is evident that those who are now out of work and unable to qualify under the insurance system must be taken care of in another way, but the insurance principle by building up a reserve in good times would help to soften the blow of unemployment when times became bad. Even a much more limited scheme, that of old age pensions, has taken 86,000 people off the labour market during the last few years. While I say that I shall vote for the bill, I wish to offer some criticism that I hope may lead to some alterations in the bill in committee.
I object first to the limited scope of the bill. Four-fifths of the people I represent will have no part or lot in it except to pay their share of the expense. Fishing, lumbering in its various branches, coal mining, pulp and paper mills and farming would include the bulk o.f the people I represent. The fisherman, the individual who owns his boat and gear, and the farmer on his own land, would not come under this bill, because it would be difficult to regard them as out of work employees. In a sense they are capitalists, although I hesitate to apply that name to them; it has become such a term of opprobrium. But when it comes to the lumber workers, those in the logging camps and the saw mills, I cannot understand why they should not be included; they are purely and simply workers. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was kind enough to suggest that he might take the temper of the house on that matter in committee, and perhaps allow them to come in. I hope he does so.
I wish to refer for a moment to the excepted employments, those which do not come under the bill. The first is employment in agriculture, horticulture and forestry. I do not know why agricultural workers should be cut out. The second exception is employment in fishing. That is ambiguous; I suppose it would cover not only the fi-herman with his own gear but a man working in a cannery or reduction plant for wages. I see no reason why they should be excluded while people working in fruit or vegetable canning factories are included. I think that is an injustice. The next exception is employment in lumbering and logging. I do not know whether the word "lumbering" would include saw mills,
(Mr. Neill.]
but I am rather afraid it would, and if so a change should be made there. Then another exempted employment is in transportation by water or by air, and stevedoring. There is a large body of men on the Pacific coast, I suppose running into thousands, who make their permanent living working on boats. They are a decent organized body, mostly married men, and live in the towns from which the boats sail. And the same applies to stevedoring; there was a time when it was a most casual form of pick-up labour, but that is not the case now. These men are well organized, have their homes and stay by their job, are fairly well paid, and I see no reason why they should not be included. They cannot be regarded as casual labourers. One would think, if the idea is to start in a safe way and keep within the recommendations of the actuaries, that the more people involved the better; because it is well known that if you spread the risk over a larger number of people it can be calculated more accurately and you are better able to meet the demands.
Another exempted employment is banking, mortgage, loan, trust, insurance or other financial business. Why is a clerk in a hardware store or a real estate or lawyer's office or a wholesale grocery to come under the act while a clerk in a bank or insurance company remains outside? Surely the odium that apparently attaches to bankers nowadays need not attach to their often underpaid employees. Then employment in domestic service is excepted unless the employed person is employed in a club or in any trade or business carried on for the purposes of gain. That means that a girl in a cafe or hotel who has an opportunity to augment her wages by tips may come under the act but her less fortunate and lower paid sister in a private house is left out. I see no justice in that. Nurses are also excluded; I see no justification for that.
I do not want to be nasty, but it looks to me rather as if this bill had been framed-

speechtext: "Framed" is right.

speechtext:
-with a very significant eye upon the eastern industrial worker, the man who works in a factory or foundry or textile industry, while we on the Pacific coast and down by the Atlantic are to be left to shift for ourselves, in the same way that the manufacturing interests in eastern central Canada are taken care of by the tariff at the expense of us in the W'est and those in the far east.
The largest body of men among my constituents w-ho w'ould come under this act

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Neill
would I presume be the coal miners, but I am a little doubtful if even they will qualify. They work intermittently, they are not fired but are simply laid off, and by that means a much larger number of men get the work spread amongst them. It is quite common for them to draw only three days' pay a week; I have known them to draw only three days' pay a fortnight. It is questionable whether they would qualify under this bill. It might be held that they are not out of employment because they are still working, although in this intermittent manner, and there is a provision that no man can get any unemployment benefit until he has been idle nine days. These men in fact are not idle nine days, although they may work only two or three days a week. There is another aspect of it that rather alarms me; it may be positively harmful to these men and others employed by large concerns both in the east and the west. Any large company, but particularly those I have in mind, coal mining companies that operate on this intermittent system, might fire half their employees. Suppose a company employs four hundred men and they are only working three days a week; the company has to pay for every man, and that would be $4,800 a year. If they fired half of them and employed the other half six days a week they would have to pay only half that sum, so that the company would save S2,400 a year. And that would apply to the big companies in the east, such as Simpson's and Eaton's, perhaps to an alarming extent. Companies often carry people not working full time just in order to keep them going.
I notice also the employer must pay for exempted people. Why draw a distinction between excepted employments and exempted people who are exempt under three specified conditions? But the employer must pay for those exempted people although the man himself is exempted and does not draw any benefit. It does not seem fair that the employer in that case should have to pay for the days he works.
Now a word as to the procedure, which seems to me complicated to say the least; and when procedure is complicated it means trouble. There are two routes by which one may proceed. Under section 27 there are five subparagraphs which cover most of the ordinary points on which disputes are likely to arise in connection with a man's employment or unemployment. These are subject to decision by the commission. Failing settlement by the commission or as an appeal from the commission they can go to the
exchequer court. There are no details as to how the employee is to get there. Going to the exchequer court is a costly thing. The exchequer court comes to the coast only at long intervals. Can you imagine a man having a dispute about S6 a week going to the exchequer court? There are no provisions to say whether the man is to have his expenses paid. The Prime Minister promised some consideration on that point. Then there is another route, a parallel one apparently'; I do not seem to be able to fit the two into each other, but it would seem that he can take one or both. The other route begins with section 28. Let us begin at the ground floor. There is a local insurance officer; he is the local man. Then there is a court of referees, provided with a specially appointed chairman. Then there is a panel to be constituted from which these referees are to be drawn. Above them there are deputy umpires and then an umpire, and above them under subsection 4 we come to the appointment of an unemployment and social insurance commission of three, of whom the Prime Minister spoke this afternoon. One would suppose that was almost enough machinery to run a petty little one-horse insurance scheme like this, but turning to section 36 you find provision made for an unemployment insurance advisory committee, consisting of a chairman and six members. They are not to be paid, but section 37 provides that they may receive an indemnity, which may amount to about $20 a day, and they will be able to run up to about $1,800 or $2,000 a year. This is not to be an unimportant thing: subsection 6 of section 37 states:
The minister may assign to the committee from the public service of Canada or otherwise such professional, technical, secretarial and
ether assistance as the committee may require . . .
So evidently they are going to operate on a considerable scale. What are they going to do; what is to be the work of this advisory committee? They are to advise the commission, and they are to report on the fund administered by the commission. That is found in subsections 1 and 2 of section 36. But why do they need to do that? We have a board of railway commissioners, a pension board, a radio commission, a biological commission and others; they do not need advisory committees. For the life of me I cannot understand why this commission should need such a committee. Then if you turn to section 43 you see that the commission itself, quite properly, is required to make a report
774	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Neill
to the government every year. Then why do they want someone to make a report on them? I cannot see it.
Then if we turn to section 38 we find the inevitable provision that is in all our acts nowadays, giving complete and arbitrary power to this commission to make regulations, or really to make laws. If you will turn to subsection (i) you will find that this commission of three have power to prescribe punishment for the violation of any regulation, including maximum and minimum fines not exceeding S50, and terms of imprisonment not exceeding three months. If that is not illegal it ought to be. Here is a body of men; we have not the slightest idea who are to compose it. They need not be lawyers, but they are to be given power to frame up a little criminal code of their own. They are not limited to the imposition of fines not exceeding $50, and in default imprisonment for three months; they can spread themselves and give anybody, for any offence however imaginary or trivial, of their own conception and defining, three months in gaol as well as a fine. I say that is wrong; I have no hesitation in saying so. I do not care whether or not it is legal. We are getting too much in the habit of turning over these arbitrary powers to these commissions.
Now I should like to say a word as to the benefits. After the man has paid in 25 cents a week for forty weeks and his emplo3'er has paid another 25 cents and the government 10 cents, because the government is obligated to pay one-fifth plus the cost of administration, the workman may get thirteen weeks at $6 a week for himself, $2.70 a week for his wife, and something for his children. I suppose those sums have been indicated by the investigation of the actuaries. But there is a benefit year prescribed, and it is provided that a man cannot get more than thirteen payments in any one year. The benefit year begins when he receives his first benefit, and he has to pay in for forty weeks before that. That will be almost a year, because at odd times he may be sick or he may have to go to his mother-in-law's funeral or something of the kind. It will take him almost a year in which to qualify. Then in the second year he may receive benefits for only thirteen weeks, and thereafter he must pay in for thirteen weeks more before qualifying for any further relief, but he can get only thirteen weeks' benefit in any one year.
That is the end of these two enactments. Again I turn to the title and quote the other things promised.
. . . for aid to unemployed persons, and for other forme of social insurance and security, and for purposes related thereto.

Now I turn to subsection 1 of section 7, which provides that this commission shall try to formulate schemes for the insurance of the excepted classes, for the assistance of people now unemployed who are not eligible under the act, for training them and so on. This might have been and should have been the very crux of the act; it is the most important part. Why has not this been done already; why are they starting only now with instructions to investigate, when this legislation has been in process of incubation for three years? Why were they not devoting their energies to the formulation of a scheme to deal with unemployment, which is more important even than the scheme under consideration? Why do they not put this other advisory committee to work and have them start at once to devote their whole time to this question?
That is enough of that. Sections 39 and 40 deal with national health, and the duties of the commission in this connection could be performed by a competent stenographer. They are to assemble reports, publications, information and data concerning any scheme, and pass it around to anyone who wants it. There is no suggestion that they do anything practical, and I understand that this is due to the fact that as the legislation referred to in the preamble does not apply to health matters because there is no treaty in that connection, it is recognized that this question can be dealt with only through the provinces. I am not finding fault with that; I am merely directing attention to it.
I should like to conclude with just one general criticism, and it applies to both the employment section and the insurance section. It is that all these appointments are to be political. At page 278 of Hansard the Prime Minister said it was his intention to make this measure non-political so far as possible. I believe that if it were left entirely to him and he had everything under his own notice that would be the case to a large extent, but unfortunately these things are not done in that way. Local political associations and so on make recommendations. It is true that the umpires must be judges, but other than that this measure presents an opportunity to make a widespread political machine. Not a single appointment is to be made by the civil service commission. Let us begin with the employment officer. He is a local man, and he is to have a local committee to guide him. See section 13. Right there you have the danger of the office being run as a political machine, or the still greater danger of having it referred to as such. Every

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. MacNicol
man who has a job he does not like or want, or any man who does not want a job, will say, "I was discriminated against because I was not on the right side of politics. Otherwise I could have found a better job." Any arrangement about which it is possible to make such remarks is going to be fatal for the men trying to find work under the scheme, fatal to the success of the office and eventually fatal to the government that would take advantage of such an opportunity. I am not making any discrimination as between one political party or another.
Dealing with the unemployment side of the bill, this unemployment advisory committee is going to be appointed and paid by the government. Then there is this commission under section 4, which is to be chosen by the government and whose salaries are to be fixed in the same way. The umpires are to be chosen by the government as well, but they are to be judges, and they are not to be paid. Then there are the chairmen of the courts of referees, who are to be chosen by the government, not even by the commission. Then we have the panels to be chosen to represent employers and contributors, but mark you this: it does not say they are to be chosen by the employers and contributors. They are to be chosen to represent them, and who is to do the choosing? It will be done by the political commission, of course. The panel gives the thing a nice sound of fairness; the panel is to be chosen to represent the employers and contributors; these panels are to be constituted, whatever that means, by the commission and from them shall be chosen the men for the courts of referees. That makes it possible to have a very fair panel, but a real political choice. It would not matter how many men were put on the panel provided the commission were wised up as to whom they should pick out of that panel. That would give a fictitious air of fairness to the thing, yet it might be political from beginning to end. I notice that the chairman and the referee courts are to be paid at the discretion of the committee. Now we come to the insurance officer, another political appointment, but curiously enough under section 28 of the bill no provision has been made to pay him at all. I suggest the section will have to be altered when we reach the committee stage. With the exception of the umpires, all these appointments are to be political. This is simply asking for trouble. The bill we are now discussing is a new departure, and a great deal depends on getting off to a good start, and the way it is handled in the early days of its operation.
By attaching to it right at the start this odour of politics it is badly handicapped. I suggest that throughout the country the measure would meet with greater approval if some of those appointments, in fact all of them, were put under the control of the civil service commission.
I hope the government may see fit to amend in committee some of the features I have criticized. Otherwise, on the general principle of the measure, I am prepared to vote for the second reading.

Mr. Speaker, may I point out that, apart from the views expressed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) who said he would support the bill, the views expressed by the other hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon and evening in opposition to the bill are not the views of men at present working in industry. On Saturday last while at home I took the opportunity to speak to foremen of quite a number of large industries in the city of Toronto, a number of which are running twenty-four hours a day. The foremen told me that the men under their charge appear to be heartily in accord with the unemployment insurance proposals offered by this government.
In his observations the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that the recommendations of several committees which had sat during his term of office and had discussed the question of unemployment insurance could not be adopted because of certain circumstances which he indicated. May I say to him however that during the same years in which the right hon. gentleman held office a number of countries throughout the world, some of which may have been labouring under conditions far worse than those obtaining in Canada, did adopt unemployment insurance legislation. Queensland, in Australia, adopted unemploj'ment insurance legislation in 1922, Russia in 1922, Italy in 1923, Poland in 1924, a number of cantons in Switzerland in 1924, Bulgaria in 1925 and Germany in 1927. Each of these states has adopted a compulsory and contributory scheme. Two other countries adopted voluntary schemes, namely Norway in 1922 and Spain in 1923. If those countries in the years I have mentioned could adopt unemployment legislation I cannot see why Canada could not have taken a similar course. I was associated with business between the years 1921 and 1929, and I have knowledge of the fact that a considerable amount of money was made during that time. During the last two or three years in which it held office the late Liberal govern-
776	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. MacNicol
ment permitted certain companies which had made enormous profits to split their stocks. I am not finding fault with the fact that some made profits; but I maintain that if some extra consideration had also been given the workers in those industries the results would have been more advantageous, and perhaps at that time a system of unemployment insurance could have been set up on their behalf.
I shall not give the names of companies, but will be content to say that in 1929 company No. 1 split its stock twenty to one; in 1929 company No. 2 split its stock eight to one; in 1928 company No. 3 split its stock six to one; in 1928 company No. 4 split its stock four to one; in 1929 company No. 5 split its stock four to one, and again in 1929 company No. 6 split its stock four to one.
I was associated with industry for a long time and I have been of the opinion that the men working in the plants were entitled to more than they were getting out of what they were producing. Long ago I concluded that unemployment insurance would be one method by which the workman would receive more than the actual wages he received for his work. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) said, in effect, that the number who would be affected by the bill is not very large. In making that observation I suggest the hon. member should have remembered that at the time the first unemployment legislation was adopted by Great Britain only 2,250,000 were affected out of a total working population of 15,000,000 or 16,000,000. This government undertakes to cover 1,701,834 workers out of a total working population less than twice this number. I say that in that regard this government at the outset has gone much farther than did the first government, namely that of Great Britain, which adopted unemployment legislation.
Lest I forget I should like to refer to something mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) this afternoon, something which filled me with hope. He made reference to taking care of those who are not protected by this measure, and alluded to the fact that he was considering the people not covered by the bill, and to whom reference was later made by the hon. member for North Winnipeg. After all, this bill is essentially an unemployment insurance bill; it is not a relief measure. It is designed to take care of men and women employed in industry who may have to suffer temporary periods of unemployment. In my humble opinion the act covers that situation satisfactorily.
It is a well known fact that in all civilized countries the worker's only source of cash supply for the maintenance of himself and

his family in health and comfort is his wages, and that when his wages are stopped because of his being thrown out of work he and his family are at once in economic jeopardy. The average worker in industry and in other vocations	has to	face	not	only	the menaceof being	thrown	out	of	work	because	oflack of work to do, but three other major economic menaces. He may be thrown out of work	because	of old	age;	he may	bethrown out of work because of invalidity; he may be	thrown	out	of	work	because	of
illness. It is for this reason that, in my opinion, on the continent of Europe-because there has been little or no advance in this kind of legislation on the American continent -the great nations help to sustain the purchasing power of their people, as I shall show later, by means of four major acts of social relief. The first is old age pensions, which I shall not discuss because we have the old age pension in this country. But this bill does provide machinery for consideration of factors affecting the national health and perhaps invalidity, and certainly it does take care of the fourth factor, namely, unemployment that results from there being no work for the workers to do.
On motion of Mr. MacNicol the debate was adjourned.
